---
title: "3. Covariates"
description: >
  Covariates by area, by time step, and by both: how to build the tables,
  how to read the coefficients, and what happens when the data cannot
  inform one.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
```

The fit of [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) had the default mean, an intercept and
a linear trend in time, and the spatial-temporal field did the rest.
Covariates move part of that variation into the mean. They can explain it,
and they let areas with the same covariate values borrow strength from each
other, including areas with no surveys.

stareal takes covariates as tables keyed by area, by time step, or by both.
This tutorial uses the crt K76T data of tutorial 1. To run without
downloads, it builds its covariates from the package's own data: a smooth
regional trend, and a contrast between Kenya and Uganda and the rest of the
region. The last section shows how to build the same tables from a raster
of your own, such as transmission intensity or elevation.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data

As in tutorial 1:

```{r data}
fr <- areal_frame(igad_adm1, id = "id", groups = c(country = "country"),
                  link_within = "country", adjacency_snap = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "year")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

## 2. Three kinds of covariate table

A covariate table is an ordinary data frame. Its key columns say what it
varies over:

| Key columns | Varies by | One row per |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | area | area |
| `time` (labels) or `t` (step numbers) | time step | time step |
| `id` and `time` (or `t`) | area and time step | area-time cell |

Every other column is a covariate, named in the formula as it is named in
the table. **A table must cover every area, every step or every cell of the
frame**, not just the surveyed ones, because `predict()` needs the
covariates everywhere. Transforms and interactions are computed as columns
first: the formula takes plain names (and `trend()`), not `log(x)` or
`x:z`.

The three tables of this tutorial:

```{r tables}
# by time: a natural spline in the year, 3 degrees of freedom
years <- as.numeric(tf$labels)
basis <- splines::ns(years, df = 3)
by_time <- data.frame(time = tf$labels, s1 = basis[, 1], s2 = basis[, 2], s3 = basis[, 3])

# by area: 1 in Kenya and Uganda, 0 elsewhere
by_area <- data.frame(id = igad_adm1$id, ku = as.numeric(igad_adm1$country %in% c("Kenya", "Uganda")))

# by area and time: ku times a linear trend from -1 in 1989 to 1 in 2024
by_cell <- expand.grid(id = igad_adm1$id, time = tf$labels, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
by_cell$ku_trend <- by_area$ku[match(by_cell$id, by_area$id)] *
  seq(-1, 1, length.out = tf$n_steps)[match(by_cell$time, tf$labels)]

head(by_time, 3)
head(by_area, 3)
c(rows = nrow(by_cell), areas = fr$m, steps = tf$n_steps)
```

`ku_trend` is built to match `trend()`, which also runs from −1 at the
first step to 1 at the last.

### Standardised or not

By default, numeric covariates are standardised: mean 0 and sd 1 over the
areas, steps or cells of their table. A coefficient is then the effect of
one sd, and the default prior on the fixed effects (normal, sd 3 on the
logit scale) suits any units. Factors become one 0/1 column per level after
the first, and are not standardised.

The covariates here are already on a unit scale, and their coefficients are
easier to read unstandardised, so the fits below use
`scale_covariates = FALSE`. With covariates in large units, such as
population or rainfall in millimetres, keep the default.

## 3. A covariate by time: a smooth regional trend

`trend()` makes the regional mean a straight line on the logit scale.
Anything else, such as a decline that starts late and then levels off, is
left to the field. A spline basis in the year lets the mean bend:

```{r fit-smooth, eval = FALSE}
long_run <- list(n_iter = 20000, n_burn = 5000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 10)
fit_smooth <- fit_areal(d, ~ s1 + s2 + s3, covariates = by_time, scale_covariates = FALSE,
                        control = long_run)
```

```{r load, include = FALSE}
cache <- readRDS("_cache/covariates.rds")
fit_smooth <- cache$fit_smooth
fit_smooth$data$frame <- fr       # the cache stores fits without their frame
fit_ku <- cache$fit_ku
fit_ku$data$frame <- fr
fit_linear <- readRDS("_cache/crt76t.rds")$fit
fit_linear$data$frame <- fr
```

```{r smooth-summary}
cache$checks$smooth$checks[, c("check", "value", "threshold", "pass")]
summary(fit_smooth)
```

The spline coefficients mean little one by one. The curve they make does:
the regional mean on the prevalence scale, draw by draw, beside the
straight line of tutorial 1. (This is the prevalence where the field is
zero, roughly the median unit, not the average over units.)

```{r smooth-curve, fig.height = 4}
curve <- function(fit, X) {
  b <- posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit)[, colnames(X)]
  p <- plogis(unclass(b) %*% t(X))
  data.frame(year = years, mean = colMeans(p),
             lo = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.025), hi = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.975))
}
X_smooth <- cbind(intercept = 1, by_time[, c("s1", "s2", "s3")])
X_linear <- cbind(intercept = 1, trend = seq(-1, 1, length.out = tf$n_steps))
both <- rbind(cbind(curve(fit_smooth, as.matrix(X_smooth)), mean_model = "spline (this tutorial)"),
              cbind(curve(fit_linear, X_linear), mean_model = "linear trend (tutorial 1)"))
ggplot(both, aes(year, mean, colour = mean_model, fill = mean_model)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "K76T prevalence, regional mean", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The straight line cannot bend. It sits below the spline from the
mid-1990s to about 2012, and above it after 2017. The spline shows the
shape the data support: K76T close to fixation from the mid-1990s to
about 2008, then a fall to under 10% by 2020. Two cautions:

- **The start rests on little.** Only 6 surveys predate 1995, 3 in Kenya
  and 3 in Sudan. The rise at the start is the spline bending where data
  are scarce, and may not be real: note how wide its interval is.
- **A regional curve is only as regional as its data.** Kenya and
  Uganda hold 60 of the 72 surveys since 2015, so the fall after 2015 is
  mostly theirs. Section 4 asks whether it applies elsewhere.

The hyperparameters change too. `rho_s` falls from 0.99 in tutorial 1 to
about 0.74, with a wide interval. The reason is in the Leroux prior: the
variance of the field's average over the whole region is proportional to
`sigma^2 / (1 - rho_s)`. With a straight-line mean, the field has to carry
the bend in the regional curve, and a `rho_s` close to 1 is what lets it.
With the bend in the mean, the field no longer needs to, and the data no
longer insist that neighbouring units be so alike. A covariate changes what
the field has to explain, so the field's parameters are only comparable
between models with the same mean.

## 4. Covariates by area, and by area and time

The country curves of tutorial 1 suggest that K76T fell sooner in Kenya and
Uganda than elsewhere. Is the difference real, or could the field have made
it by chance? `ku` shifts the level in Kenya and Uganda, measured at the
middle of the window, where `trend()` is 0. `ku_trend` changes their slope:

```{r fit-ku, eval = FALSE}
fit_ku <- fit_areal(d, ~ trend() + ku + ku_trend, covariates = list(by_area, by_cell),
                    scale_covariates = FALSE, control = long_run)
```

Several tables go in as a list. Each covariate must be in exactly one of
them.

```{r ku-summary}
cache$checks$ku$checks[, c("check", "value", "threshold", "pass")]
summary(fit_ku)
```

The posterior probability that the decline was steeper in Kenya and Uganda
is the share of draws with `ku_trend` below zero:

```{r ku-prob}
b <- posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit_ku)
mean(b[, "ku_trend"] < 0)
```

The probability is close to 1. The decline was steeper in Kenya and
Uganda, and the field, which could have produced a local decline on its
own, does not account for the difference. Read the coefficients together:

- `trend` is now the slope outside Kenya and Uganda: half the change in
  logit prevalence from 1989 to 2024. Its interval spans zero widely.
  Outside the two countries, recent surveys are few, so the data cannot pin
  down a slope there. Of the surveys since 2015, 60 are in Kenya and
  Uganda, and 12 elsewhere: 11 in Sudan and 1 in Ethiopia.
- `trend + ku_trend` is the slope in Kenya and Uganda, about −4.7: a fall
  of more than 9 on the logit scale over the window.
- `ku` is near zero: at the middle of the window, around 2006, the two
  countries were not different from the rest.

The hyperparameters barely move from tutorial 1's. `sigma` drops a little,
from 2.5 to 2.3, as the contrast takes over part of the variation; the field
still carries the rest.

## 5. A factor level with no data

Why not a covariate for every country? Somalia has no crt surveys, so the
data say nothing about a Somalia effect. `fit_areal()` says so before
it starts sampling:

```{r uninformed}
by_country <- data.frame(id = igad_adm1$id, country = igad_adm1$country)
tryCatch(fit_areal(d, ~ trend() + country, covariates = by_country, control = list(verbose = FALSE)),
         warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
```

The posterior of `countrySomalia` would be its prior, and every prediction
for Somalia would carry that prior's uncertainty, on top of the field's.
Three remedies:

- **Merge the level** with others, as `ku` does for the countries outside
  Kenya and Uganda.
- **Give it an informative prior**, by name:
  `priors = areal_priors(beta_sd = c(countrySomalia = 0.5))`.
- **Leave the covariate out** and let the field carry the differences
  between countries, as in tutorial 1.

The first level of a factor is its baseline, and is alphabetical by
default. Here that is Djibouti, which has a single survey. Choose a
well-surveyed baseline with
`factor(country, levels = c("Kenya", ...))`.

## 6. Predicting with covariates

Nothing changes: `predict()` evaluates the covariates in every area and
year from the tables the fit was given.

```{r predict}
pr_ku <- predict(fit_ku, groups = "country", verbose = FALSE)
pr_linear <- predict(fit_linear, groups = "country", verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r predict-compare, fig.height = 4.5}
countries <- c("Kenya", "Uganda", "Ethiopia", "Sudan")
cmp <- rbind(cbind(pr_linear$groups$country, model = "~ trend() (tutorial 1)"),
             cbind(pr_ku$groups$country, model = "~ trend() + ku + ku_trend"))
cmp <- cmp[cmp$id %in% countries, ]
ggplot(cmp, aes(date, mean, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "K76T prevalence", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

In Kenya and Uganda the two models agree: the data there decide. After
2015 they part in Ethiopia and Sudan. In the second model, the steep fall
belongs to Kenya and Uganda alone, so Ethiopia and Sudan, with few recent
surveys, keep a prevalence near 50% in 2024, against about 20%, with much
wider intervals. Neither answer comes from data on those countries. Each
follows from what the mean assumes where the surveys stop. A covariate
changes the map most where the data are thinnest, which is where it most
needs to be right.

Whether either covariate model predicts better than tutorial 1's is a
question for [cross-validation](crossval.html), which compares the three on
the same held-out surveys.

## 7. Your own covariates from a raster

Most real covariates come as rasters: transmission intensity, rainfall,
elevation, population. `exactextractr` averages a raster over each
polygon, and a raster with one layer per year gives a table by area and
year:

```{r raster, eval = FALSE}
r <- terra::rast("my_covariate.tif")             # one layer per year, named "2000", "2001", ...
ex <- exactextractr::exact_extract(r, igad_adm1, "mean")
by_cell <- data.frame(id = rep(igad_adm1$id, times = ncol(ex)),
                      time = rep(sub("^mean[.]", "", names(ex)), each = nrow(ex)),
                      my_covariate = unlist(ex, use.names = FALSE))
```

Two things to settle before fitting:

- **Coverage.** The table must cover every year of the time frame. A raster
  that starts later than the surveys needs a stated rule for the earlier
  years, such as holding the first year's value, or a shorter time frame.
- **Area, not survey.** A covariate here describes an area in a year, and
  must be known for every one of them. Properties of a survey (the study
  design, the sampled population) are not covariates of this model.
